title: Dallas clinic to pay $7.5 million over COVID-19 testing overbilling allegations
text:
Dallas clinic to pay $7.5 million over COVID-19 testing overbilling allegations
Aymancare PLLC, a Dallas-area medical clinic, agreed to pay $7.5 million to resolve allegations that it violated the False Claims Act by overbilling the federal government for COVID-19 testing services provided to uninsured patients, according to an Aug. 26 announcement from United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas, Ryan Raybould.
“Aggressively investigating and pursuing healthcare fraud is a top priority for my office,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “We will use all available tools, including through civil enforcement mechanisms like the False Claims Act, to identify and recover any healthcare dollars lost to fraud, waste or abuse—the American taxpayer deserves no less.”
Jason E. Meadows, Special Agent in Charge of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, said, “Ensuring that federal funds dedicated to the COVID-19 response are used appropriately remains a core oversight priority for HHS-OIG. Billing for services that were never provided is a blatant abuse of the health care system and diverts critical resources away from patients who genuinely need them. We will continue working with our law enforcement partners to hold accountable those who exploit federal programs and to safeguard taxpayer dollars.”
The United States alleged that Aymancare operated pop-up testing sites during the pandemic advertising free COVID-19 tests paid by a federal program supporting uninsured patients through the Health Resources and Service Administration’s reimbursement initiative. Authorities say Aymancare not only billed for specimen collection and testing but also charged separately for evaluation and management services as if additional treatment was performed when no such separate services occurred; only nasal swabs were administered by technicians or other personnel.
The resolution resulted from coordinated efforts between the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas—which prosecutes federal crimes, manages civil litigation on behalf of the government, promotes community trust through outreach initiatives, employs around 100 assistant attorneys and support staff across several offices in northern Texas serving about eight million residents—and its partners at HHS-OIG, according to information on its official website.
Officials highlighted ongoing efforts under national initiatives like the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and National Fraud Enforcement Division aimed at combating fraud in federal programs through False Claims Act enforcement.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Brian Stoltz handled this matter. The settlement resolves civil claims which remain allegations only; there has been no determination of civil liability.
